native.scale_note: 1 unit = 1 cm. Gross dimensions are approximate authored teaching dimensions: crown about 11 mm wide and 7.5 mm high, roots about 14 mm long. Comparison teeth are drawn at 58% of the local source scale. The periodontal ligament has a nominal source band of 0.30 mm; cementum is deliberately widened for visibility (nominal mature field about 0.28–0.58 mm before the cervical taper and mesh smoothing). These field values are not post-build thickness measurements. Artery/vein calibre, spacing and shallow section-face offsets (0.28 and 0.58 mm above the canal) are schematic; no complete capillary bed is depicted. Isolated coronal dentin-pulp specimen is uniformly enlarged 100× relative to the gross tooth: 1 displayed unit corresponds to 100 micrometres there. Specimen is 68 micrometres wide and 175 micrometres tall, a local inner-dentin sample rather than total dentin thickness.

teaching_recipe.display_name: Tooth: gross anatomy and dentin-pulp histology
teaching_recipe.summary: Preserved mandibular molar/jaw section and adult tooth types, locally repaired venous junctions and socket lining, with one isolated 100×-enlarged coronal dentin-pulp specimen.

parts.name: Enamel
parts.description: The hardest substance in the body: ~96 % hydroxyapatite in long prisms (rods), secreted by ameloblasts that are lost when the tooth erupts – so enamel cannot regrow. It covers the anatomical crown, defined by its enamel rather than by the movable gum margin, is thickest over the cusps (~2.5 mm) and thins to nothing at the neck, where it meets cementum at the cementoenamel junction (cervical line). Acid from plaque bacteria dissolves it (caries); fluoride mainly reduces demineralization and promotes remineralization, making the repaired surface more acid-resistant. Mineral recovery is not regrowth of a lost enamel volume.

parts.name: Dentin
parts.description: Bone-like tissue (~70 % mineral) forming the bulk of the tooth, under enamel in the crown and cementum on the root. It is pierced by dentinal tubules containing processes of the odontoblasts that line the pulp, so it is living and sensitive: exposed dentin (recession, worn enamel) hurts with cold and sweet (hydrodynamic theory), and odontoblasts slowly deposit secondary dentin during life, narrowing the pulp space. Injury can instead stimulate tertiary dentin: reactionary dentin from surviving odontoblasts, or reparative dentin from new odontoblast-like cells after greater injury. These cellular responses are explained, not resolved by this gross mesh.

parts.name: Pulp chamber (coronal pulp)
parts.description: Soft connective tissue in the pulp cavity of the crown, with horns reaching up under each cusp. Odontoblasts line its surface; it contains fibroblasts, stem cells, blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves (Aδ fibres for sharp pain, C fibres for dull, throbbing pain). Carious dentin can trigger pulpal defense and inflammation before a pulp horn is directly exposed; direct exposure is another route of injury. The drawn horns show gross tissue relationships, not a complete microscopic vascular or nerve plexus. It shrinks with age as dentin is added.

parts.name: Root canals (radicular pulp)
parts.description: The pulp cavity continues down each root as the root canal (the mesial root of a lower first molar usually has two canals, mesiobuccal and mesiolingual, the distal root one or two). Nerves and vessels enter through the apical foramen. Root canal treatment (endodontics) removes infected pulp, shapes and disinfects the canals and seals them with gutta-percha, saving a tooth with irreversible pulpitis or a dead pulp. This model uses one simplified longitudinal radicular pulp route per root in a mesiodistal teaching section. Do not count these visible routes as a full three-dimensional canal inventory: additional buccolingual canals, isthmuses and accessory branches are not represented.

parts.name: Cementum
parts.description: A thin layer of bone-like tissue covering the root dentin from the neck to the apex, thickest near the apex (cellular cementum with cementocytes). Collagen (Sharpey's) fibres of the periodontal ligament are anchored in it. It is deposited throughout life, which compensates for occlusal wear, and is exposed when the gum recedes (root caries, sensitivity).

parts.name: Apical foramen
parts.description: An opening in the apical region connects radicular pulp with the surrounding tissues and transmits vessels and nerves; its position can differ from the geometric root tip. The selectable brown part marks cementum bordering the apical region, not an empty object filling the opening. The neurovascular routes already pass through source-fitted clearances. A necrotic infected pulp can affect the periapical tissues; this static opening alone does not demonstrate how inflammation compromises blood flow or establish a radiographic diagnosis.

parts.name: Periodontal ligament
parts.description: A 0.15–0.4 mm layer of dense collagen fibres (Sharpey's fibres) slung between cementum and the bony socket wall: the tooth is suspended in its socket by a fibrous joint (gomphosis). It acts as a shock absorber, carries mechanoreceptors that sense biting force, and its cells remodel the socket – the basis of orthodontic tooth movement. It is destroyed in periodontitis; on X-ray it is the thin dark line round each root.

parts.name: Alveolar bone proper (lamina dura)
parts.description: The thin plate of compact bone lining the socket (alveolus), perforated by vessels and nerves (cribriform plate) and receiving the periodontal ligament fibres. It shows as a continuous white line round the root on dental X-rays; its loss at the apex signals periapical infection. Bone of the alveolar process exists only to hold teeth and resorbs after extraction.

parts.name: Cortical bone of mandible
parts.description: Dense compact bone forms the outer mandibular plates and inferior border around the tooth-bearing region. This local section shows the bony socket setting and its relationship to cancellous bone and the mandibular canal. Plate thickness and root relationships should not be treated as universal measurements from this schematic block. The mylohyoid muscle and deep fascial spaces are absent, so the model does not establish a specific route of infection spread or select an anaesthetic technique.

parts.name: Cancellous (spongy) bone
parts.description: A lattice of trabeculae between the cortical plates, supporting the sockets and carrying the dental vessels and nerves to the root apices; the interradicular septum between the two roots and the interdental septa between teeth are made of it.

parts.name: Bone marrow
parts.description: Marrow in the spaces of the spongy bone – largely fatty (yellow) in the adult mandible, with islands of haemopoietic (red) marrow. Infection spreading from a dead tooth through the marrow causes osteomyelitis of the jaw; radiotherapy and antiresorptive drugs (bisphosphonates) predispose to osteonecrosis after extractions.

parts.name: Mandibular canal
parts.description: A tunnel lined by a thin shell of cortical bone running forward through the body of the mandible below the root apices, carrying the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle from the mandibular foramen toward the anterior mandible. A mental branch exits near the premolars while an incisive neural continuation remains within bone. It carries the inferior alveolar nerve, artery and vein. Only a short local segment is modelled here; its open block ends are intentional specimen boundaries, not new foramina. Patient-specific relationships to molar roots require clinical imaging and are not measured by this teaching block.

parts.name: Inferior alveolar nerve & dental nerves
parts.description: Branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) running in the mandibular canal; its dental branches enter each apical foramen and form a plexus in the pulp (plexus of Raschkow) under the odontoblasts. Pulpal nerves signal only pain, whatever the stimulus. Its terminal distribution includes the mental nerve, which exits to the lower lip and chin, and an incisive continuation within the mandible supplying anterior teeth. Those anterior terminations lie outside this local molar block. The drawn branches indicate supply routes; the microscopic Raschkow plexus is not resolved.

parts.name: Inferior alveolar artery & dental arteries
parts.description: Branch of the maxillary artery (external carotid) running with the nerve in the mandibular canal; small dental arteries pass through each apical foramen into the pulp, and others supply the periodontal ligament and bone. Below-root dental branches are widened and slightly separated on the section face for legibility; their displayed calibre, spacing and surface offset are schematic. The artery is presented on the exposed canal face; the vein routes behind the nerve at its canal crossing. Above the canal, arteries and veins are exposed at separate shallow schematic section-face offsets (0.28 and 0.58 mm), not anatomical displacements. No capillary bed is depicted.

parts.name: Inferior alveolar vein & dental veins
parts.description: Drains the pulp, periodontium and bone to the pterygoid venous plexus. Venous return leaves the pulp through apical openings alongside its incoming arterial supply. This static pair identifies inflow and outflow; it does not resolve the microcirculation or demonstrate the sequence of vascular compression during pulp inflammation. Below-root dental branches are widened and slightly separated on the section face for legibility; their displayed calibre, spacing and surface offset are schematic. The artery is presented on the exposed canal face; the vein routes behind the nerve at its canal crossing. Above the canal, arteries and veins are exposed at separate shallow schematic section-face offsets (0.28 and 0.58 mm), not anatomical displacements. No capillary bed is depicted.

parts.name: Gingiva
parts.description: The gingiva forms a free collar and an attached region around the tooth-bearing alveolar process. Its outer oral epithelium is keratinized or parakeratinized masticatory epithelium; sulcular and junctional epithelia are normally nonkeratinized. The gingival sulcus ends at the junctional epithelium, which attaches to the tooth through an internal basal lamina and hemidesmosomes. These microscopic layers are explained but are not separately resolved in this gross gum mesh. Plaque-induced gingivitis is inflammation of the gingiva; periodontitis includes destruction of periodontal attachment and supporting bone. Probing depth alone is not a diagnosis, and the model does not predict pocket severity from its drawn sulcus.

parts.name: Alveolar mucosa
parts.description: Thin, red, loosely attached, non-keratinised lining mucosa below the mucogingival junction, continuous with the floor of the mouth and the cheek. It moves with the lips and cheeks; flaps for surgery and local anaesthetic infiltrations are placed here.

parts.name: Incisor – crown
parts.description: Anatomical crown: the enamel-covered portion ending at the cementoenamel junction; the clinical crown is the portion exposed above the gum margin. Incisors (8 in the adult, 2 per quadrant – central and lateral): chisel-shaped crowns with a straight incisal edge for cutting and nipping food, and a single conical root. Lower central incisors are the first deciduous teeth to erupt (~6–10 months) and the permanent ones erupt at 6–7 years.

parts.name: Incisor – root
parts.description: Root: covered by cementum and held in its socket by the periodontal ligament. Incisors (8 in the adult, 2 per quadrant – central and lateral): chisel-shaped crowns with a straight incisal edge for cutting and nipping food, and a single conical root. Lower central incisors are the first deciduous teeth to erupt (~6–10 months) and the permanent ones erupt at 6–7 years.

parts.name: Canine – crown
parts.description: Anatomical crown: the enamel-covered portion ending at the cementoenamel junction; the clinical crown is the portion exposed above the gum margin. Canines (cuspids, 4 in the adult): a single pointed cusp for piercing and tearing and the longest root of any tooth (the upper canine's reaches up beside the nose – 'eye tooth'), which makes it a stable anchor at the corner of the arch.

parts.name: Canine – root
parts.description: Root: covered by cementum and held in its socket by the periodontal ligament. Canines (cuspids, 4 in the adult): a single pointed cusp for piercing and tearing and the longest root of any tooth (the upper canine's reaches up beside the nose – 'eye tooth'), which makes it a stable anchor at the corner of the arch.

parts.name: Premolar – crown
parts.description: Anatomical crown: the enamel-covered portion ending at the cementoenamel junction; the clinical crown is the portion exposed above the gum margin. Premolars (bicuspids, 8 in the adult, 2 per quadrant): a large buccal and a smaller lingual cusp for crushing and grinding; usually one root (the upper first premolar often two). There are no deciduous premolars – they replace the deciduous molars.

parts.name: Premolar – root
parts.description: Root: covered by cementum and held in its socket by the periodontal ligament. Premolars (bicuspids, 8 in the adult, 2 per quadrant): a large buccal and a smaller lingual cusp for crushing and grinding; usually one root (the upper first premolar often two). There are no deciduous premolars – they replace the deciduous molars.

parts.name: Molar – crown
parts.description: The anatomical crown is enamel-covered and ends at the cementoenamel junction; the clinical crown is the exposed portion above the gum margin. Molars (12 in the adult including the four third molars or wisdom teeth): broad occlusal surfaces with 3–5 cusps for grinding; lower molars have two roots (mesial and distal), upper molars three (two buccal, one palatal). First permanent molars erupt at ~6 years behind the deciduous teeth – often mistaken for milk teeth – and third molars at 17–21 years, often impacted.

parts.name: Molar – neck
parts.description: The neck (cervix) marks the transition between anatomical crown and root at the cementoenamel junction. The gingival margin and junctional epithelial attachment are separate soft-tissue landmarks whose relationship to this junction can change with eruption and recession. The narrow comparison band is a selectable teaching region of the tooth, not an added tissue layer. Recession can expose root surfaces and increase the clinical crown without moving the cementoenamel junction.

parts.name: Molar – roots
parts.description: The roots, covered by cementum, are held in the alveolar sockets by the periodontal ligament. Molars (12 in the adult including the four third molars or wisdom teeth): broad occlusal surfaces with 3–5 cusps for grinding; lower molars have two roots (mesial and distal), upper molars three (two buccal, one palatal). First permanent molars erupt at ~6 years behind the deciduous teeth – often mistaken for milk teeth – and third molars at 17–21 years, often impacted.

parts.name: Histology – tubular mineralized dentin
parts.description: Local inner coronal dentin with explicitly open tubular bores. Specimen uniformly enlarged 100× relative to gross model; 1 displayed unit is 100 micrometres. This is a sectional sample, not the complete dentin thickness.

parts.name: Histology – predentin
parts.description: Unmineralized organic predentin between odontoblast cell bodies and mature dentin. A schematic 18-micrometre band with continuing tubules. 100× display enlargement.

parts.name: Histology – odontoblast bodies and processes
parts.description: Peripheral columnar odontoblasts with a connected fine process entering the adjoining predentin/dentin tubule. Processes end within the sampled inner dentin; this is not a claim that every process spans full dentin thickness. Cytoplasm is separated from nuclear volumes for sectional readability. 100× display enlargement.

parts.name: Histology – odontoblast nuclei
parts.description: Basally placed elongated nuclei fitted inside actual constructed odontoblast meshes before cytoplasm/nucleus domain separation. Front row is intentionally sectioned longitudinally. 100× display enlargement.

parts.name: Histology – pulp connective-tissue matrix
parts.description: Loose connective-tissue support at the coronal pulp periphery. Matrix is fitted around cells. Local field is simplified, without a complete cell-rich/free-zone arrangement or vascular/nerve plexus.

parts.name: Histology – pulp fibroblasts
parts.description: Sparse spindle connective-tissue cells in the sampled pulp, distinct from the odontoblast layer. Front-face section exposes fitted nuclei; cell number is illustrative rather than a density measurement.

parts.name: Histology – fibroblast nuclei
parts.description: Nuclei fully contained in their actual constructed spindle fibroblast bodies before domain separation.
